issues.description: The UML diagram in the problem statement labels the class as `Course` while the textual description, tasks, template repository, and solution repository all refer to and provide a `Lecture` class. This name mismatch in the UML can confuse students about which class they should implement and which attributes/methods the UML refers to.
issues.suggested_fix: Update the UML diagram in the problem statement to name the class `Lecture` (instead of `Course`) so it matches the textual description, the template class, and the solution. Alternatively, if the intended class name is `Course`, update the text and template to use `Course` consistently. The simplest fix preserving educational intent is to rename the UML class to `Lecture`.

issues.description: The problem text and provided code refer to a Lecture class (e.g., "implement a class that represents a lecture", and the template/solution both contain Lecture.java), but the UML in the problem statement names the class "Course". This inconsistency (Course vs Lecture) can confuse students about which class they are expected to implement and map the UML attributes to, creating unnecessary cognitive load when relating the UML to the starter code.
issues.suggested_fix: Make the UML class name consistent with the rest of the exercise by renaming the UML entry from "class Course" to "class Lecture" (and ensure any UML references/diagrams use "Lecture"). This aligns the diagram with the problem text and the provided template/solution code and removes the naming ambiguity for students.
